new_statements.quote: p. 418: "Stress in Bul falls on the penult unless there is a paragogic vowel, in which case it falls on the antepenult. Loss of the paragogic syllable in Bul therefore results in regular penult stress." n. 15, p. 425: "The Holle list (Stokhof 1983:139-181) shows stress placement in Bul. This is identical with the word stress pattern in Kdp. It is probable that in pre-PGtl stress regularly fell on the penult. With the development of the paragogic vowel stress thus became unpredictable (as in Kdp and, until this change, in Bul). In Gtl stress again became regular by shifting from the antepenult to the penult in words containing a paragogic syllable."
new_statements.citation: Sneddon, James N. & Hunggu Tadjuddin Usup. 1986. Shared sound changes in the Gorontalic language group: implications for subgrouping. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 142(4): 407-426.
new_statements.locator: p. 418 (section 3, change 19, PDF p. 13) and endnote 15, p. 425 (PDF p. 20); Kaidipang described on p. 409 (PDF p. 4)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: text layer (the PDF's metadata). PDF p. 13 = printed p. 418: the text layer reads exactly 'Loss of the paragogic vowel but not etymological vowel in word-final position can probably be accounted for in terms of stress placement. Stress in Bul falls on the penult unless there is a paragogic vowel, in which case it falls on the antepenult. Loss of the paragogic syllable in Bul therefore results in regular penult stress.15' (section 3, change 19). PDF p. 20 = printed p. 425, note 15: the text layer reads '.. It is probable that in pre-PGtl stress regularly feil on the penult..'; I rendered the page at 200 dpi and the printed word is 'fell', so the reader's quote matches the printed page verbat…
new_statements.relation_note: Kaidipang has no catalog record and no existing stress statement, so this is a new statement rather than a confirmation or contradiction. It is second-hand for Kaidipang: the primary observation is the Holle list's stress marking for Buol, and Kaidipang is brought in by the assertion that its pattern is 'identical' (Usup is a North Sulawesi native speaker-linguist, so the assertion is informed, but no Kaidipang stress data are printed). It also implies penult stress for Gorontalo (Gtl), consistent with what the catalog family expects for that language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kaidipang (Kdp) is said to have the same word-stress pattern as Buol: stress on the penult, except that words ending in a paragogic (echo) vowel added after an etymological final consonant carry stress on the antepenult, i.e. on the penult of the pre-paragogic stem. Because the paragogic vowel is not distinguishable on the surface from an etymological final vowel, the authors call Kaidipang stress 'unpredictable'; synchronically it is a lexically determined choice between penult and antepenult, historically regular penult stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The only stated deviation from penult stress is antepenult stress in words with a paragogic final vowel. No other exceptions, no loanword remarks, no mention of vowel length interacting with stress (n. 16 says the phonemic status of length has not been examined).
new_statements.identity_note: Sneddon & Usup 1986 p. 409: "Kaidipang (Kdp). This is spoken in the north-west of Bolaang-Mongondow district.. There are two dialects, usually referred to as Kaidipang and Bolaang Itang, with a total of about 24,000 speakers. The dialects are very closely related and there appear to be no differences in their phonological systems." The stress remark is made for Kdp as a whole, not for one dialect; the Kaidipang Holle list is Stokhof 1983:217-239.

readall_conflicts: Within the one listed work there is no internal disagreement. There is a subgroup-level tension with two papers already held by the project from the earlier reading (not in this task's works list, both opened and checked here): Lobel 2016, LD&C 10, p. 399 ("As in other Mongondow-Gorontalo languages, stress is not contrastive in Ponosakan, and regularly falls on word-final syllables, with a few unpredictable exceptions where it falls on the penultimate syllable") and Lobel & Paputungan 2017, LD&C 11, p. 334 ("Similar to the other Mongondow-Gorontalo languages, stress is not contrastive in Lolak.. stress in Lolak regularly falls on the word-final syllable"). Those describe Mongondow-branch languages and generalise to the whole Mongondow-Gorontalo group without naming Kaidipang; if the generalisation were applied to Kaidipang it would differ from Sneddon & Usup both in placement (final vs penult/antepenult) and in type (predictable non-contrastive vs 'unpredictable'). Sneddon & Usup's statement is specific to Kaidipang and should carry more weight, but it is itself an inference from Buol data, so the placement for Kaidipang rests on one sentence in a footnote. The Usup et al. 1999/2000 Kamus Bahasa Indonesia-Kaidipang front-matter phonology sketch (held by the project) says nothing about tekanan/stress.

sources.note: p. 334 §2.1 Stress: 'Similar to the other Mongondow-Gorontalo languages, stress is not contrastive in Lolak, in contrast to most of the core Central Philippine languages such as Tagalog, Cebuano, and Bikol. … stress in Lolak regularly falls on the word-final syllable, even in Indonesian loanwords where it would be expected to fall on the penultimate syllable instead.' Again subgroup-level for non-contrastiveness; placement stated for Lolak only; Kaidipang not named.

sources.note: p. 399: 'As in other Mongondow-Gorontalo languages, stress is not contrastive in Ponosakan, and regularly falls on word-final syllables, with a few unpredictable exceptions where it falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g., siˈene [siˈʔene] "who".' Subgroup-level remark (Ponosakan is Mongondow branch, Kaidipang is Gorontalic); Kaidipang not named; the final-stress placement is asserted for Ponosakan only.

sources.note: Pendahuluan §7 'Informasi Singkat tentang Bahasa Kaidipang' (pp. xiv-xvii; PDF pp. 14-17) gives the segmental phoneme chart, phonotactics (all words vowel-final, syllable pattern -(K)V-(K)V, nasal clusters), a phonemic short/long vowel contrast (tala vs taalo), /d/~/r/ variation, two allophones of /l/, and moK- morphophonemics; it lists the earlier Kaidipang studies (Usup 1971, Usup et al. 1979, 1993, 1994). Nothing at all on stress/tekanan. downloaded from the the Internet Archive capture (2024-04-16) of repositori.kemdikbud.go.id/23737/1/…; live repository unreachable.
